title: Guitar lessons with Jordan
description: Demo conversation (synthetic, for the demo account). Alex tells Jordan about starting guitar lessons to learn Saltwater by Harbor Kites, they compare practice habits with running habits, take a music-theory tangent on chords versus the band's open tunings, and return to the lesson plan.

utterances.text: Okay, don't laugh. I started guitar lessons.
I'm not laughing. I'm smiling with my whole face. Since when?
Two weeks. I finally bought one after the concert.
Let me guess. You want to play Saltwater.
Obviously. My teacher laughed when I asked. She said everyone walks in with one song.
Can you play it yet?
The first four chords, very slowly. It sounds like Saltwater if Saltwater were lost in a parking lot.
That still counts. So what's the lesson plan?
Half an hour a week with her, then fifteen minutes every day at home. Chords first, then switching between them, then strumming.
Fifteen minutes a day? That's nothing.
That's her whole point. Small and every day beats one big session on Sunday.
Wait, that's literally running. I've been telling you that for months.
I know! It's the same thing. Easy runs most days, nothing heroic.
Consistency over intensity. Your fingers are doing base mileage. Do you track it like your runs?
Little calendar on the fridge. A check mark for running, a star for guitar. I hate breaking a streak.
Okay, nerd question. Do you know why it never quite sounds like the record?
Because I'm bad?
Partly. But I read that their guitarist barely uses standard tuning. He drops the low string down to a D, and some songs are in a fully open tuning.
Wait, what does that even mean?
In normal tuning, every chord is a shape you make with your fingers. In an open tuning, the strings already make a chord when you strum them with no fingers at all.
So that's why their songs have that ringing, droney thing.
Exactly. The open strings keep ringing under everything. That's the Harbor Kites sound, especially on Night Ferry.
So chords are the shapes, and the tuning changes the whole instrument underneath.
Pretty much. Your teacher's going to have to retune you.
That's going on my list for Thursday. Okay, back to the lesson plan. This month, the four chords clean, no buzzing. Next month the strumming pattern, then maybe the drop D version.
And by the half marathon?
I'll play the chorus at the finish line. Badly.
I'll hold the speaker.
